**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The cursor blinks, a silent metronome counting down the seconds until I must begin. A thousand words—a vast expanse, yet so finite. What do I fill it with? The weight of expectation presses against my ribs, a quiet insistence that whatever I write must matter.

But what does matter? The grand, sweeping narratives of history? The intimate, whispered secrets of a single life? Or perhaps the mundane, the overlooked—the way sunlight slants through a window at 3:47 PM, casting shadows that no one else notices?

I think of the first time I understood the power of words. I was eight, sitting cross-legged on a library floor, a book splayed open in my lap. The story was about a girl who found a door in a tree, and when she stepped through, the world tilted. I remember the way my breath hitched, the way my fingers trembled as I turned the page. Words had done that. Words had made me believe in magic.

Now, as an adult, I know that words are both magic and weapon. They can build bridges or burn them. They can heal or wound. They can make a stranger feel seen or make a loved one feel invisible. A thousand words is a gift, a responsibility. What do I do with it?

Perhaps I should write about the ocean. The way it stretches endlessly, indifferent to human sorrow. The way it swallows light and spits it back as something new. The ocean does not care if we name it or measure it or drown in it. It simply is. There is a comfort in that, a kind of brutal honesty.

Or maybe I should write about the woman I saw on the subway last week. She was hunched over, her hands clutching a paper bag with something greasy staining the bottom. Her shoes were worn, her coat too thin for the weather. She didn’t look up once, not even when the train lurched and sent her stumbling into the man beside her. He muttered something, annoyed, and she shrank further into herself. I wanted to say something—to her, to him, to the whole car—but I didn’t. Words failed me then. They often do.

A thousand words. I could list every fear I’ve ever had. The irrational ones (spiders in my hair, the earth suddenly opening beneath me) and the rational ones (loneliness, irrelevance, the slow erosion of time). I could write about the way my mother’s hands look now, the veins more pronounced, the skin thinner, as if she is slowly becoming translucent. I could write about the first time I realized my parents were mortal, that they would not always be there to shield me from the world’s sharp edges.

But perhaps it’s better to write about joy. The way my dog greets me as if I’ve been gone for years, even if I’ve only stepped out for milk. The way my best friend laughs so hard she snorts, and how that sound is one of the few things that can make me forget, even for a moment, that the world is on fire. The way a perfect sentence can make my chest ache, the way a song can unravel me.

A thousand words. I could fill them with anger. The way the world is broken, the way we keep breaking it. The way we look away when it’s easier, when it’s convenient. The way we tell ourselves stories to sleep at night, even when we know they’re lies.

But anger is exhausting. And I am tired.

So instead, I will write about the quiet moments. The way my grandmother hums when she cooks, the way my father still holds my mother’s hand after forty years. The way the first sip of coffee in the morning feels like a promise. The way, sometimes, when I’m very still, I can almost hear the universe breathing.

A thousand words. I have used most of them now. The cursor still blinks, patient, waiting. I wonder if any of this mattered. I wonder if it ever does.

But then I remember the girl on the library floor, the way her eyes widened as she read about a door in a tree. And I think, maybe, that’s enough.
